questions.q: What does a Neo4j label represent, and what is it roughly analogous to in the relational world?
options: A category attached to a node, roughly analogous to a table name
A unique identifier for each node, like a primary key value
A type of relationship between two nodes
A stored procedure attached to a node
questions.explain: Labels categorize nodes (e.g. Customer, Employee), and a single node can carry more than one label at once.

questions.q: In Neo4j, what are true statements about every relationship between two nodes?
options: A relationship can have multiple types simultaneously
Relationships cannot carry any properties
Relationships have no direction and no type
It is always directed (has a start and end node) and always typed (has exactly one relationship type)
questions.explain: Every Neo4j relationship is directed and has exactly one type, written in ALL_CAPS by convention, such as PURCHASED or REPORTS_TO.

questions.q: What genuinely surprises relational-trained DBAs about properties in Neo4j, per this lesson?
options: Properties can only exist on nodes, never on relationships
Properties can live on both nodes and relationships, not just on entities
Properties must always be integers
Only one property is allowed per node
questions.explain: A relationship like PURCHASED can itself carry properties such as date and quantity, data that relationally would require a separate junction table.

questions.q: Why doesn't a graph traversal get proportionally slower as the total database grows, according to this lesson's explanation of index-free adjacency?
options: Neo4j caches the entire database in memory at all times
Relationships are stored as direct physical pointers between nodes, so traversal cost depends on the pattern matched, not total database size
Graph databases don't actually store relationships at all
Traversal speed is unrelated to how relationships are stored
questions.explain: Because relationships are stored objects with direct pointers rather than resolved via a JOIN, traversing to a neighbor is a constant-time lookup regardless of overall graph size.

questions.q: Per this lesson's honest framing, which of the following is still typically better handled by a relational or document database than a graph database?
options: Product recommendations based on what similar customers bought
Multi-hop fraud detection through chains of accounts
Simple lookups by a single known key and heavy aggregate reporting across large flat datasets
Org-chart traversal of direct and indirect reports
questions.explain: The lesson is explicit that graphs aren't the better tool for everything — simple key lookups and flat aggregate reporting are still typically simpler or better relationally.
